A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Live Avatar, with matching research objectives and identifiable methods and experiments. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive revision and reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original GenBench and AVSpeech evaluations, efficiency and stability ablations, 10,000-second generation results, and a 20-participant user study.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark and user-study results, together with additional experiments on training convergence, denoising steps, block size, cache-noise scheduling, and quantization.

M1.justification: v4 introduces noisy motion-frame scaffolding in Stage 1 through a frozen FramePack encoder, then removes it for Stage 2; v1 explicitly removes FramePack and lacks this conditioning branch. Algorithm 4 also changes the AAS broadcast from decoded output to the generated latent. The underlying Self-Forcing, TPP, and Rolling RoPE framework remains.

E1.justification: Both versions use AVSpeech training and held-out evaluation, GenBench short and long videos with the same character and composition coverage, 10,000-second extrapolation, and human perceptual evaluation. The later ablations and hardware measurements vary configurations within this retained task coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated avatar-baseline memberships remain unchanged, including Hallo3, which already appears in v1's tables. v4 Table 6 adds fix-noisy-kv-cache at t=557 alongside the existing clean-cache comparator, providing a limited but substantive extension of the cache-scheduling comparison.

E3.justification: Stage 2 training changes from 2,500 to 500 steps, and v4 specifies an optimized FP8 inference configuration for its principal results. Table 3 revises non-TPP controls and GPU counts. New protocols vary denoising steps, latent-block size, and precision, and introduce T.Flicker evaluation and H20 runtime measurements. These changes preclude treating all revised scores as same-configuration improvements.

E4.justification: v4 adds controlled studies of motion-frame scaffolding convergence, 2–4 denoising steps, 1–4 latent frames per block, and FP8 versus FP16 inference. It extends the cache-noise analysis with fixed-noise and flicker measurements and adds visual stability ablations. The 10,000-second test already existed in v1; the earlier short-video cache comparison is no longer reported.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and mean normalized ratings from 20 participants without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The new convergence plot likewise provides no uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Results are extensively revised under the changed training and inference configurations. Full-system FPS/TTFF changes from 20.88/2.89 seconds to 45.2/1.21 seconds; AVSpeech FID/FVD changes from 64.00/532.52 to 48.91/502.37. User-study naturalness falls from 86.3 to 80.1, while synchronization rises from 80.6 to 86.0 and consistency from 91.1 to 93.2. Long-rollout scores are updated and new ablation results are added.

T1.justification: The flow-matching equations, DMD gradient, and autoregressive formulation in Equations 1–5 remain substantively unchanged. v4 adds conceptual arguments about noisy caches and static scenes, but no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: v4 adds motion-frame scaffolding and its claimed fivefold distillation-convergence speedup as a central contribution. It strengthens the headline system claim from approximately 20 FPS to 45 FPS with 1.21-second TTFF and elevates the existing GenBench benchmark to a standalone contribution. The overarching 14B streaming and infinite-length generation claim is retained.

C2.justification: v4 expands the stability explanation with a static-scene assumption, noise-filtering arguments, and noisy-cache distribution-drift reasoning. It explicitly acknowledges reduced naturalness associated with accelerated motion in the distilled model. Its limitations now identify reliance on largely unchanged scenes and approximately three-second end-to-end latency that remains inadequate for bidirectional real-time interaction.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds detailed FP8 scaling and precision exceptions, attention-kernel selection, compilation, LoRA merging, streaming VAE caching, offloading, and memory information. v4 also specifies motion-frame noising and expands AAS/RoPE implementation details. It promises future GenBench and evaluation-script release without establishing current availability; v1's approximately 500-GPU-day training estimate is removed.

R1.justification: v4 adds references supporting scaffolding, noise-based explanations, and evaluation, including History-guided Video Diffusion, VBench, DINOv2, and Z-image, while dropping Phased DMD and OmniHuman-1.5. It sharpens its criticism of Self-Forcing and LongLive. These are targeted changes within the retained positioning around large-model streaming, efficiency, and long-horizon stability.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, training explanation, stability discussion, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Long-video generation now precedes TPP, the user study moves to the appendix, and references move before the supplementary material. These changes substantially reorganize the argument beyond accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: The two-column main paper becomes a single-column layout. Figure 2 is redrawn to include scaffolding, new Figures 5–6 present stability examples and convergence, and new tables cover denoising steps, block size, and quantization. Table 3 becomes a component matrix, while existing user-study and supplementary displays are relocated and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation of central design choices through the cache-scheduling, convergence, step-count, block-size, and precision controls, while documenting the optimized execution path in enough detail to make its efficiency claims more assessable. The explicit scene and interaction-latency limitations also improve claim calibration. Lower reported naturalness and conflicting default TTFF values in Tables 3/5 versus Table 10 remain weaknesses, but the gains in experimental support and implementation transparency provide a substantial net improvement.
